name: Elisha
bio:
Elisha son of Shaphat, of Abel Meholah, was named by the LORD at Horeb as the prophet who would succeed Elijah (1 Kings 19:15-16). Elijah found him plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, working the twelfth pair himself, and threw his cloak over him without a word. Elisha ran after Elijah asking only to first kiss his father and mother goodbye; Elijah's reply — "Go back again: for what have I done to thee?" — left the choice entirely his own. Elisha then slaughtered his own yoke of oxen, burned the plowing equipment to cook the meat, and gave it to the people to eat — a decisive break with his old life — before leaving to become Elijah's attendant (1 Kings 19:19-21).

## 📖 Core Story: Receiving Elijah's Mantle

On Elijah's last day, Elisha refused three times to leave his side as the LORD sent Elijah from Gilgal to Bethel, to Jericho, and to the Jordan, where Elijah parted the water with his cloak so the two could cross on dry ground. Asked what he wanted before Elijah was taken, Elisha requested a double portion of Elijah's spirit — a hard thing, Elijah told him, granted only if Elisha witnessed the taking. He did: a chariot and horses of fire appeared, Elijah went up in a whirlwind, and Elisha, crying "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof," tore his own clothes and took up Elijah's fallen cloak (2 Kings 2:1-12).

Elisha struck the Jordan with the cloak, asking, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" and the water parted for him just as it had for Elijah — proof to the watching sons of the prophets at Jericho that Elijah's spirit now rested on him, and they bowed before him (2 Kings 2:13-15). At Jericho, he healed the city's bad water by casting salt into its spring in the LORD's name (2 Kings 2:19-22). On the road up to Bethel, youths jeered at him, calling him "bald head"; he cursed them in the LORD's name, and two bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23-24).

## 📖 Core Story: Water in the Desert

When Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom marched against the rebelling Mesha, king of Moab, and their armies nearly died of thirst in the wilderness, Jehoshaphat insisted on consulting a true prophet of the LORD, and Elisha was found. Elisha told Jehoram bluntly that he wouldn't even look at him if not for Jehoshaphat's presence, but at a minstrel's playing the LORD's hand came upon him, and he prophesied the dry valley would fill with water and Moab would be delivered into their hands — a prophecy fulfilled exactly, with water filling the land by morning and the Moabite army routed and their land devastated (2 Kings 3:9-25).

## 📖 Core Story: Miracles of Provision and Life

A widow of one of the sons of the prophets cried to Elisha that her creditor was coming to take her two sons as slaves; with nothing in her house but a pot of oil, Elisha told her to borrow empty vessels from her neighbors and pour her oil into them. The oil didn't stop flowing until every vessel was full, giving her enough to sell and pay her debt with plenty left to live on (2 Kings 4:1-7).

At Shunem, a well-off woman recognized Elisha as a holy man and built him a small room on her roof so he could stay whenever he passed through. Through his servant Gehazi, Elisha learned she had no son and her husband was old, and promised she would embrace a son within the year — which she did, despite her disbelief (2 Kings 4:8-17). Years later the boy died suddenly of a sudden headache; the Shunammite laid him on Elisha's bed and rode to find Elisha at Mount Carmel, refusing to say what was wrong until she reached him and grabbed his feet. Elisha sent Gehazi ahead with his staff to lay on the child's face, but nothing happened. Elisha himself went in, shut the door, prayed, and stretched himself over the child's body twice; the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes, and Elisha gave him back to his mother alive (2 Kings 4:18-37).

During a famine at Gilgal, a pot of stew was made poisonous by wild gourds a servant had mistakenly gathered; Elisha neutralized it by adding flour, and no harm came to anyone who ate it (2 Kings 4:38-41). When a man brought Elisha twenty barley loaves and fresh grain, Elisha had his servant set it before a hundred men despite having far too little food, declaring the LORD's word that they would eat and have some left over — and they did (2 Kings 4:42-44).

## 📖 Core Story: Healing Naaman the Leper

Naaman, the leprous commander of Syria's army, came to Israel seeking healing on a servant girl's advice, carrying a letter and a fortune for whoever could cure him. Elisha, hearing the king of Israel panic over the request, told him to send Naaman along instead. When Naaman arrived with his chariots at Elisha's door, Elisha didn't even go out to him, sending a messenger with the simple instruction to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman left furious at being treated so plainly, but his servants persuaded him to try it anyway; he dipped seven times and his flesh was restored, healed completely (2 Kings 5:1-14).

Naaman returned declaring there was no God but Israel's, and tried to press a gift on Elisha, who flatly refused to accept anything — "As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none." Naaman left in peace with two mule-loads of earth instead, meaning to worship only the LORD from then on. Elisha's servant Gehazi, however, secretly ran after Naaman and lied to obtain silver and clothing in Elisha's name. When Gehazi returned, Elisha confronted him for it and pronounced that Naaman's leprosy would now cling to Gehazi and his descendants forever — and Gehazi left Elisha's presence a leper (2 Kings 5:15-27).

## 📖 Core Story: Floating Axes, Blinded Raiders, and a Besieged City

When one of the sons of the prophets lost a borrowed axe head in the Jordan while cutting wood, Elisha cut a stick, threw it in, and made the iron float to the surface (2 Kings 6:1-7). During Syria's war with Israel, Elisha repeatedly warned the king of Israel of the Syrian king's planned ambush locations, saving him again and again, until the frustrated Syrian king learned it was Elisha leaking his plans and sent an army by night to surround him at Dothan. When Elisha's servant panicked at the sight of the surrounding army, Elisha prayed that his eyes be opened, revealing the hills full of fiery chariots and horsemen on their own side. Elisha then prayed the Syrians blind, led the blinded army into Samaria itself, and had their sight restored only once they realized where they were. Rather than let the king kill them, Elisha insisted they be fed and sent home, and Syrian raids stopped for a time (2 Kings 6:8-23).

When Ben-Hadad later besieged Samaria and famine grew so severe that a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and people resorted to cannibalism, the horrified king of Israel blamed Elisha and swore to behead him. Elisha, forewarned, had the elders bar the door against the king's messenger, calling the king "this son of a murderer" (2 Kings 6:24-33).

## 📖 Core Story: Deliverance from the Famine

Elisha prophesied that within a day, amid the crushing famine, flour and barley would sell cheaply at Samaria's gate. A royal officer scoffed that this couldn't happen even if the LORD opened windows in heaven; Elisha told him he would see it happen but not live to eat any of it. That night, four leprous men, desperate enough to risk the Syrian camp rather than starve, found it abandoned — the LORD had made the Syrians hear the sound of a great army and they'd fled in panic. After looting and hiding plunder from tent to tent, the lepers realized they should report the good news, and the famine ended exactly as Elisha had said. The scoffing officer, now in charge of the gate, was trampled to death by the rushing crowd — he saw the abundance with his own eyes but, as Elisha had foretold, never tasted it (2 Kings 7:1-20).
